title: Personal pronouns, sum, and first sentences

objectives.can: Parse the forms of ego, tu, nos, vos and the forms of is used for 'he, she, it'.
Parse the present, imperfect and future indicative of sum.

explanation.summary: The pronouns of the first and second persons, *ego* and *tu*, and the verb *sum*, 'I am', let you read the shortest complete sentences of the Bible. Latin does not need a pronoun with a verb, since the ending already gives the person, so an expressed *ego* or *tu* usually carries emphasis.

sections.heading: Ego and tu
body: The pronouns of the first person (*ego*, 'I') and the second person (*tu*, 'you', one person) have their own case forms, different for singular and plural. They have no gender: the same form is used of a man or a woman. The plural of *ego* is *nos*, 'we'; the plural of *tu* is *vos*, 'you' (several people).

The forms are irregular and must be learned. The nominative, *ego* and *tu*, is rarely needed with a verb, because the ending of the verb shows the person. When it is there, it stresses the subject: in *Ego sum*, 'I am (the one)'; in *tu es Petrus*, 'you are Peter (and no one else)'.

The ablative of these pronouns joins to *cum* as an ending: *mecum*, *tecum*, *nobiscum*, *vobiscum*. The genitive of *ego* and *tu* is not used for 'my' and 'your'. For that Latin uses the adjectives *meus* and *tuus*, which you have met.

sections.heading: Is, ea, id: he, she, it
body: Latin has no separate pronoun for the third person. The demonstrative *is* (feminine *ea*, neuter *id*) does that work. In the nominative it is seldom used for 'he', since the verb's ending says it. In the other cases it is common: *eum* ('him'), *eos* ('them'), *ejus* ('his', 'her', 'of him'), *eorum* ('their'), *eis* ('to them').

Unlike *ego* and *tu*, *is* has three genders, which agree with the noun it stands for: *eum* is masculine, *eam* feminine, *id* neuter. The genitive *ejus* is the same for all three genders, and it serves as 'his', 'her' or 'its'. Remember that it is a genitive and does not agree with the thing owned. *Nomen ejus* is 'his name' or 'her name' according to who is meant.
The analysis often leaves the gender of these forms undecided, because the form is the same for several. The questions ask for case and number, and for gender only when it is certain.

sections.heading: The verb sum, 'I am'
body: *sum* is the verb 'to be'. It is the commonest verb in Latin, and it is irregular: its stems are es- and fu- and its endings are only partly regular. It serves in two ways. It can mean 'exist', and it can join a subject to a complement as a link: in *Deus caritas est* the verb joins *Deus* and *caritas*, both in the nominative. A noun or adjective used like this is called a predicate nominative.

The present tense is *sum, es, est, sumus, estis, sunt*. Singular first person, *sum*: 'I am'. Second person, *es*: 'you are'. Third person, *est*: 'he, she, it is'. The plural is *sumus*, *estis*, *sunt*. The indicative mood is the ordinary statement mood. In the generated table of this lesson the cell for the second person and the first person singular may be empty: the analysis leaves *es* undecided between indicative and imperative ('be!') and does not accept *sum* as certain, although both occur in the texts.

sections.heading: Imperfect and future of sum
body: The imperfect describes a past state or continuing action: 'was' or 'used to be'. It is formed from the stem er- with the endings -am, -as, -at, -amus, -atis, -ant. So *erat* is 'he was' and *erant* is 'they were'. John begins with it: *In principio erat Verbum*.

The future uses the same stem with different endings: -o, -is, -it, -imus, -itis, -unt. So *erit* is 'he will be' and *erunt* is 'they will be'. Note the third person plural *erunt*, with -u- where the imperfect has -a- (*erant*).

A note on the exercises. In the library's analysis these imperfect and future forms are unsure: the analyser could not always choose between a form of *sum* and another reading. For that reason the generated questions in this lesson use the present tense, where the analysis is certain, and the imperfect and future are tested with questions on real verses.

sections.heading: Sum with the dative: possession
body: Latin often says that someone has something with *sum* and the dative of the owner: the thing is the subject and the owner is in the dative. Luke says of Elizabeth and Zechariah *Et non erat illis filius*, 'and there was no son to them', that is, 'they had no son'. The dative shows the owner, and the subject of the verb is the thing owned.

misunderstandings: The form *es* is 'you are', but the imperative 'be!' has the same spelling. The sentence tells which; the library's analysis shows both readings for it, which is why it is not asked for its mood.
The pronoun *ejus* does not agree with the noun it follows. It is a genitive: 'of him'. The adjectives *meus* and *tuus* do agree with the thing owned.
*vos* is not the singular. Latin 'you' is *tu* for one and *vos* for several; there is no polite plural for one person in the Vulgate.

*sum* also serves as a helping verb: in a form such as *creatus est* it combines with a participle to make a passive tense, and then it does not mean simply 'is'. The questions on *est* and *sunt* may show such sentences; a later lesson treats them.
*erit* ('will be') and *erat* ('was') differ by one letter. Check the vowel before the ending: -a- is imperfect, -i- is future.

deeper.heading: The pronouns in the other cases
body: The genitive plurals *nostrum* and *vestrum* are used for 'of us' and 'of you' after words meaning 'some' or 'each', as in 'one of you'. *nostri* and *vestri* are used for the object of a feeling, as in 'love of us'. This lesson does not ask for them.

quoted.title: Matthew
quoted.english: And I say to thee: That thou art Peter; and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *ego* and *tu* are nominatives, expressed for emphasis. *tibi* is the dative of *tu*, 'to you'. *es* is the second person singular present of *sum*: *tu es Petrus*, 'you are Peter', with *Petrus* as the predicate nominative.

quoted.title: 1 John
quoted.english: Dearly beloved, we are now the sons of God; and it hath not yet appeared what we shall be. We know, that, when he shall appear, we shall be like to him: because we shall see him as he is.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *sumus* is first person plural present: 'we are'. *est* is third person singular, 'is'. The same verse also has the future *erimus*, 'we shall be': *nunc filii Dei sumus* ('now we are children of God') against *quid erimus* ('what we shall be').

examples.analysis: *est* twice, both third person singular present: 'where your treasure is, there your heart is also'. The first *est* has *thesaurus* as its subject and the second has *cor*; each time the verb comes before its subject.

segments.english: And they asked him: What then? Art thou Elias? And he said: I am not. Art thou the prophet? And he answered: No.

segments.english: They said therefore unto him: Who art thou, that we may give an answer to them that sent us? What sayest thou of thyself?

segments.english: He said: I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, make straight the way of the Lord, as said the prophet Isaias.
